title: {{NAME}} and Princess Wren's Runaway Zoo
moral: The best adventures happen when you help someone else with theirs.

pages.content:
The princess arrived at {{NAME}}'s door on a Tuesday afternoon, looking remarkably unbothered for someone with a peacock on her head.

"I am Princess Wren," she announced. "Three of my royal animals have escaped the palace and I need a tracking expert. My butler says you are the best in the neighbourhood."

"I'm nine," said {{NAME}}.

"Precisely," said the princess. "Will you help or not?"

pages.content:
The escaped animals were: one miniature horse who adored shiny things, one tortoise who had been walking since Tuesday and was now possibly in the next postcode, and one very clever monkey named Pip who had taken the royal television remote.

{{NAME}} studied the clues methodically. Tiny hoofprints led toward the park fountain. Slow tortoise tracks went east.

From the library on the corner came the unmistakeable sound of every channel changing at once.

"I know where to start," he said.

pages.content:
They retrieved Pip from the library first (he had settled on a nature documentary and refused to change it), then found the miniature horse at the fountain wearing a stolen necklace.

The tortoise was harder. They found him at four o'clock, placidly making his way through the park rose garden.

"He escapes every Tuesday," Princess Wren admitted. "I think he likes roses."

"Then grow some roses at the palace," said {{NAME}}.

The princess stared at him. "That is the most obvious solution I have ever heard and I cannot believe my royal advisors didn't think of it."

pages.content:
Back at the palace gates, Princess Wren counted her animals: tortoise, horse, monkey, peacock. All present.

She turned to {{NAME}} with great dignity, adjusted her tiara, and said: "You are officially appointed Royal Animal Tracker, First Class."

She pinned a gold badge to his jacket. It had a tiny pawprint on it.

{{NAME}} looked at it. "Do I get paid?"

"You get invited to all the royal animal parties," said Princess Wren.

"Deal," said {{NAME}}.

pages.content:
{{NAME}} walked home as the street lights came on, his new badge catching the glow.

Pip the monkey had, at some point, slipped something into his jacket pocket. He found it now: the television remote.

{{NAME}} laughed so hard he had to sit on a garden wall to recover.

In his room that night, he set the badge on his bedside table and lay in the dark, still smiling.

Downstairs, the television switched on by itself. On the screen: a nature documentary about peacocks.
